metadata.title: A Structured Survey of Quantum Computing for the Financial Industry

problem_domains.description: Optimization of asset allocation, including Markowitz-style portfolio selection and more complex constrained variants.
problem_domains.quote: First quantum applications for the ﬁnancial industry involving optimization, simulation, and machine learning problems have already been proposed and applied to use cases such as portfolio management, risk management, and pricing derivatives.

problem_domains.description: Finding portfolios that maximize return for a given level of risk under classical Markowitz portfolio theory, including unconstrained and binary/QUBO formulations.
problem_domains.quote: All papers examine portfolio optimization under classical Markowitz portfolio theory [76]. The problem of identifying the portfolio that maximizes return for a given level of risk (formulated as the standard deviation of returns) is a central task of classical portfolio theory.

problem_domains.description: Clearing and settling as many transactions as possible or maximizing the total value of settled transactions under legal and operational constraints.
problem_domains.quote: Transaction clearing is one further use case of quantum computing. The clearing house’s goal is usually to settle as many transactions as possible or to maximize the total value of settled transactions, but this is a difﬁcult optimization problem due to a combination of legal frameworks and additional options.

problem_domains.description: Computation of risk metrics such as Value-at-Risk, Conditional VaR, and credit risk more quickly or accurately.
problem_domains.quote: A quantum computer could also be used to calculate risk metrics such as Value-at-Risk (VaR), Conditional VaR (CVaR) or credit risk.

problem_domains.description: Valuation of derivatives and bonds, including complex and illiquid instruments, potentially faster and with more factors than classical Monte Carlo.
problem_domains.quote: Another application is in the pricing of ﬁnancial derivatives, which can be complicated functions of market prices.

problem_domains.description: Modeling and predicting financial crises using complex models with many interacting agents and behavioral components.
problem_domains.quote: Quantum computers could make better predictions of ﬁnancial crises.

problem_domains.description: Broad asset management challenges that pose computational difficulties for classical computers.
problem_domains.quote: Furthermore, they point to three areas of ﬁnancial ser- vices, where problems currently arise that pose a challenge for classical computers. These areas include asset management, investment banking, and retail and corporate banking.
problem_domains.location: Section II-E Fields of quantum computing in ﬁnance

problem_domains.description: Computationally challenging problems in investment banking identified as potential targets for quantum computing.
problem_domains.quote: These areas include asset management, investment banking, and retail and corporate banking.
problem_domains.location: Section II-E Fields of quantum computing in ﬁnance

problem_domains.description: Selecting relevant features for financial models using quantum machine learning.
problem_domains.quote: In [21], the authors see potential applications in features selection, product recommendations, arbitrage, portfolio management, derivative pricing, risk analysis, credit scoring, fraud detection, anti- money laundering, and forecasting ﬁnancial crashes.
problem_domains.location: Section II-E Fields of quantum computing in ﬁnance

problem_domains.problem: secure digital communication and money transfer (cryptography risk)
problem_domains.description: Threat to cryptographic foundations of secure digital communication, money transfer, and digital signatures used in finance.
problem_domains.quote: The author writes that many areas such as secure digital communication, money transfer, and signature of digital documents are based on concepts of cryptography. Using a quantum computer to break cryptography would have a major impact on our economy and society.
problem_domains.location: Section II-F Impact of quantum computing on the ﬁnancial industry

problem_domains.description: Finding optimal portfolios of financial assets, including under constraints and for index tracking.
problem_domains.quote: They try to ﬁnd the optimal portfolio of two main stock indices, the Nikkei225 and the S&P500 indices.

problem_domains.description: Markowitz-style portfolio optimization with additional constraints such as no short selling and budget limits.
problem_domains.quote: Kerenidis et al. [80] describe the case of positive portfolio optimization (no short selling) and budget constraints.

problem_domains.description: Periodic asset management to maintain portfolio characteristics over time, subject to computationally heavy optimization.
problem_domains.quote: The last of our ﬁve papers relating to portfolio optimization is by Hodson et al. [82] and deals with portfolio rebalancing which is of special relevance for institutional investors.

problem_domains.description: Selecting a subset of assets so that portfolio returns closely follow a reference index.
problem_domains.quote: Finally, it is worth mentioning the index tracking problem, which is a variant of the portfolio optimization problem. The index tracking problem aims to select a few assets so that the resulting portfolio’s return is as close as possible to a given reference index.

problem_domains.description: Optimizing securities settlement in capital markets to clear as many transactions or as much value as possible under legal and optionality constraints.
problem_domains.quote: They focus on securities settlement in the capital markets. By transaction settlement, they refer to the process by which securities (tradable ﬁnancial assets such as shares, bonds and derivatives) are delivered in exchange for payment.

problem_domains.description: Pricing various financial derivatives, especially complex and path-dependent ones, more efficiently than with classical Monte Carlo.
problem_domains.quote: Rebentrost et al. [40] discuss the Black-Scholes-Merton model [89], [90], which considers the pricing of options, which are a fundamental subset of ﬁnancial derivatives.

problem_domains.description: Valuing derivatives whose payoff depends on the entire path of the underlying asset, which is computationally expensive.
problem_domains.quote: Path-dependent derivatives, on the other hand, are much more difﬁcult to price than path-independent derivatives because they require an often computationally expensive payoff calculation at multiple points in time on each path, so minimizing the number of paths required for this step would lead to a signiﬁcant advantage in the pricing process.

problem_domains.problem: pricing interest rate derivatives with HJM model
problem_domains.description: Valuing interest rate derivatives under the multi-factor Heath-Jarrow-Morton model with many stochastic factors.
problem_domains.quote: The multi-factor Heath-Jarrow-Morton (HJM) model [91] is widely used in ﬁnance for the valuation of interest rate derivatives. However, the main problem in building an HJM model to describe the development of the yield curve is the large number of degrees of freedom.

problem_domains.description: Estimating portfolio risk measures such as Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk, especially with nonlinear payoff structures.
problem_domains.quote: Woerner and Egger [10] present in their paper a quantum algorithm that analyzes risk measures such as VaR. Speciﬁcally, they show how to use quantum AE to evaluate the risk measures VaR and Conditional VaR (CVaR) on a gate-based quantum computer.
problem_domains.location: Page 12, Section E. Estimating Risk Measure(s)

problem_domains.description: Estimating the difference between VaR and expected loss, also known as economic capital requirement.
problem_domains.quote: In a follow-up paper, Egger et al. [96] build on this work and use a very similar approach, and thus also show a theoretical quadratic speed-up to estimate the difference between the VaR and the expected loss value. This risk measure is also known as the economic capital requirement.

problem_domains.description: Forecasting financial crashes in complex financial networks by identifying asset value changes that cause large drops in institutions’ market value.
problem_domains.quote: The question is what change in the value of the assets could cause a massive drop in the market value of the institutions, i.e., a ﬁnancial crash.
problem_domains.location: Page 12–13, Section F. Predicting Financial Crashes

solution_approaches.approach: Optimization
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum optimization methods to solve financial optimization problems such as portfolio optimization and transaction settlement.
solution_approaches.quote: In [1] the following three main ﬁelds of application are discussed: • Optimization • Machine learning • Monte Carlo methods
solution_approaches.location: Section II-E Fields of quantum computing in ﬁnance

solution_approaches.approach: Monte Carlo / Simulation
solution_approaches.description: Quantum-accelerated Monte Carlo or simulation methods for tasks like risk measure estimation and derivative pricing.
solution_approaches.quote: In [2] the same categorization is employed, but the more general term "Simulation" instead of "Monte Carlo" is used.
solution_approaches.location: Section II-E Fields of quantum computing in ﬁnance

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) and Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE/QPA)
solution_approaches.description: Searching and counting algorithms used as core subroutines for Monte Carlo-type estimation of statistical properties.
solution_approaches.quote: Brassard et al. [35] present generalizations of Grover’s search algorithm, called "Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE)" and "approximate counting", which can be used to estimate the number of items in a set fulﬁlling a certain condition and are core subroutines in quantum computation for various applications.

solution_approaches.approach: HHL algorithm (solving linear equation systems)
solution_approaches.description: Use of the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd algorithm and variants to solve linear systems arising in portfolio optimization and machine learning.
solution_approaches.quote: Harrow et al. [38] propose an algorithm for solving systems of linear equations.
solution_approaches.location: Section III-B3b) Solving linear equation systems

solution_approaches.approach: quantum machine learning (including qPCA and recommendation systems)
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms for machine learning based on linear systems solvers, including quantum principal component analysis and fast recommendation systems.
solution_approaches.quote: The Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm has lead to several propositions for general-purpose fast ma- chine learning using quantum algorithms (e.g., Kerenidis and Prakash [41], Kerenidis et al. [42], Allcock et al. [43] or N. Liu and Rebentrost [44]), including a quantum version of principal component analysis [45] (qPCA).
solution_approaches.location: Section III-B3b) Solving linear equation systems

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Interior Point Method (QIPM) for optimization
solution_approaches.description: Quantum versions of interior point methods for semi-definite, cone, and linear programming with potential quadratic speed-up.
solution_approaches.quote: Improvements to solve optimization prob- lems such as semi-deﬁnite programs via a quantum version of the interior point method (QIPM) have been proposed by [47]–[49].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QUBO)
solution_approaches.description: Hybrid quantum-classical approximate optimization algorithms, often formulated as QUBO/Ising problems, for combinatorial optimization in finance.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms [51], [52], [54] serve to ﬁnd approximate solutions faster than the currently known classical algorithm by exploiting quan- tum ﬂuctuations [55], i.e., tunnelling effects between local minima. Amongst the most widely used algorithms for this type of procedure are the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) [56] and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Al- gorithm (QAOA) [57].

solution_approaches.approach: QUBO / Ising model formulation
solution_approaches.description: Encoding financial optimization problems as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problems that map to the Ising model for use with VQE, QAOA, or quantum annealers.
solution_approaches.quote: A special form of combinatorial optimization problems are so- called Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. They unify a variety of combinatorial optimization problems that are often encountered in the ﬁnancial industry. QUBO can be mapped to the Ising model, which allows the ap- plication of quantum algorithms such as VQE or QAOA [59].

solution_approaches.approach: gate-based quantum computers
solution_approaches.description: Use of universal gate-based quantum computers to implement algorithms like QAE, HHL, VQE, and QAOA for financial applications.
solution_approaches.quote: Most of the algorithms discussed above are intended for gate-based quantum comput- ers.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum annealers
solution_approaches.description: Use of adiabatic/annealing hardware based on the Ising model to solve financial combinatorial optimization problems.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum annealing is based on a general result of quantum mechanics known as the adiabatic theorem (quantum annealing is also known as adiabatic quan- tum computation [69]).

solution_approaches.approach: noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) algorithms
solution_approaches.description: Hybrid and noise-tolerant algorithms designed to run on current noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers for near-term financial applications.
solution_approaches.quote: However, it is possible that noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers will ﬁnd in- teresting applications far before general-purpose, fault-tolerant quantum computing is available [17].

solution_approaches.approach: quantum Monte Carlo speed-up via amplitude estimation
solution_approaches.description: Use of amplitude estimation to reduce the number of samples required in Monte Carlo-based financial computations.
solution_approaches.quote: They described that it has been shown that full-scale fault-tolerant (gate-based) quantum computers provide a signiﬁcant speed- up by drastically reducing the number of samples required compared to classical Monte Carlo methods [71], [72].

solution_approaches.approach: quantum annealer portfolio optimization (QUBO)
solution_approaches.description: Formulating portfolio optimization as a QUBO and solving it on a quantum annealer and hybrid solver.
solution_approaches.quote: [77] describe the implementation of the problem on a quantum annealer and its hybrid solver... and formulate the case also as a QUBO problem.

solution_approaches.approach: reverse quantum annealing protocol
solution_approaches.description: Using an optimized reverse annealing protocol on a quantum annealer for portfolio optimization.
solution_approaches.quote: The optimized reverse annealing protocol turns out to be more than 100 times faster than the corresponding forward quantum annealing (as described by Phillipson and Bhatia [77]) on average.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum SOCP interior-point method (QIPM for SOCPs)
solution_approaches.description: Reducing constrained portfolio optimization to SOCPs and solving via a quantum SOCP interior-point method.
solution_approaches.quote: Kerenidis et al. [80] reduce this problem to Second Order Cone Programs (SOCPs)... The problem can be further solved by considering the quantum SOCP interior-point method of Kerenidis et al. [81].

solution_approaches.approach: QAOA for portfolio rebalancing with soft constraints
solution_approaches.description: Applying the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm to a soft-constrained portfolio rebalancing formulation.
solution_approaches.quote: They formulated two approaches, one with soft constraints and the Quantum Approximate optimization Algorithm (QAOA),

solution_approaches.approach: quantum alternating operator ansatz for portfolio rebalancing with hard constraints
solution_approaches.description: Using the quantum alternating operator ansatz to handle hard constraints in discrete portfolio rebalancing.
solution_approaches.quote: and another with hard constraints and the quantum alternating operator ansatz.

solution_approaches.approach: QAOA and VQE for index tracking (variational quantum optimization)
solution_approaches.description: Numerically simulating QAOA and VQE as quantum optimization algorithms within a pruning method for index tracking.
solution_approaches.quote: They numerically simulate the application of quantum optimization algorithms such as QAOA and VQE to this problem, and compare the performance of different quantum variational optimization algorithms in their pruning method.

solution_approaches.approach: hybrid quantum/classical heuristics for Mixed Binary Optimization (MBO)
solution_approaches.description: Extending VQE and QAOA to MBO problems with inequality constraints via a hybrid quantum/classical heuristic.
solution_approaches.quote: The main contribution of Braine et al. [86] is the introduction of an approach to extend the existing quantum methods (VQE and QAOA) to more general Mixed Binary Optimization (MBO) problem classes. They use a hybrid quantum/classical heuristics to address MBO problems which allows one to model optimization with inequality constraints with a quantum computer.

solution_approaches.approach: amplitude estimation (AE) for option pricing
solution_approaches.description: Preparing probability distributions and payoff functions on a gate-based quantum computer and using amplitude estimation to price options.
solution_approaches.quote: Their most important contribution is the use of the amplitude estimation (AE) algorithm, which can theoretically achieve a quadratic speed-up in the number of steps required to estimate the corresponding price compared to the Monte Carlo approach.

solution_approaches.approach: gate-based AE implementations with error mitigation for option pricing
solution_approaches.description: Implementing AE-based option pricing circuits on quantum devices with simple error mitigation schemes.
solution_approaches.quote: they show the implementation of the quantum circuits required to generate the input states and operators needed by AE to price the different option types, and apply a simple error mitigation scheme.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum principal component analysis (qPCA) for factor reduction in HJM
solution_approaches.description: Using qPCA to reduce the number of stochastic factors in the HJM model for interest rate derivative pricing.
solution_approaches.quote: Martin et al. [87] show how to apply quantum principal component analysis (qPCA) to reduce the number of stochastic factors to ﬁnd the fair price of a interest rate derivative.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum AE for VaR and CVaR
solution_approaches.description: Using quantum amplitude estimation on a gate-based quantum computer to evaluate VaR and CVaR.
solution_approaches.quote: Speciﬁcally, they show how to use quantum AE to evaluate the risk measures VaR and Conditional VaR (CVaR) on a gate-based quantum computer.

solution_approaches.approach: quantum AE for economic capital requirement
solution_approaches.description: Applying a similar AE-based approach to estimate the difference between VaR and expected loss.
solution_approaches.quote: Egger et al. [96] build on this work and use a very similar approach, and thus also show a theoretical quadratic speed-up to estimate the difference between the VaR and the expected loss value.

solution_approaches.approach: QUBO formulation and quantum annealing for crash prediction
solution_approaches.description: Constructing a QUBO representation of a nonlinear financial network model and solving it with a quantum annealer.
solution_approaches.quote: Orús et al. [17] propose a nonlinear network model for ﬁnancial markets to predict such ﬁnancial crashes. Their main contribution is the efﬁcient construction of a QUBO formula (see also Section IV-B) representing the problem. They also show how to ﬁnd a solution using a quantum annealer.

solution_approaches.approach: implementation of crash prediction QUBO on quantum annealer
solution_approaches.description: Implementing the crash prediction algorithm on a D-Wave quantum annealer as a proof of concept.
solution_approaches.quote: Y . Dinget al. [97] then implemented this proposed algorithm on a quantum annealer.

problem_solution_mappings.quote: Optimization problems are the core of many ﬁnancial problems for portfolio optimization or rebalancing. These kinds of problems are thus seen as potential use cases of quantum computing.
Rebentrost and Lloyd [79] use the HHL algorithm and its variations to describe the theoretical implementation to iden- tify the minimum risk portfolio for a given desired return.

Phillipson and Bhatia [77] and Venturelli and Kondratyev [78] restrict to a binary optimization problem, i. e. assets can either be included in the portfolio or not. This type of optimization problem is also called Quadratic Unconstrained Binary optimization (QUBO) problem.

A quantum computer could also be used to calculate risk metrics such as Value-at-Risk (VaR), Conditional VaR (CVaR) or credit risk. The beneﬁt of using a quantum computer is that these measures can be calculated faster or more accurately.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) and Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE/QPA)
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Approximate counting is especially useful to estimate statis- tical properties of a sample such as it is ‘traditionally’ often done by Monte Carlo methods.

In addition, pricing bonds and derivatives using a quantum computer instead of classical Monte Carlo simulation could contribute to a more accurate valuation, especially for less liquid traded derivatives and bonds with complex payout structures and contract terms.
Quantum computers could help to calculate complex models that take into account many actors with their complex decision-making processes and their interrelationships.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: quantum machine learning (including qPCA and recommendation systems)
problem_solution_mappings.quote: The speed-up achieved by the quantum machine learning algorithms depends on the type of problem to be solved, but may be polynomial or even superpolynomial [33]. 10 To apply any of the above quantum machine learning algorithms requires, however, for the problem to be formulated in a very speciﬁc form.
problem_solution_mappings.location: Section III-B3b) Solving linear equation systems

problem_solution_mappings.approach: Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms (VQE, QAOA, QUBO)
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Most applications related to optimization or portfolio optimization are based on approxi- mate optimization. This is explained by the fact that quantum annealing is mainly used for optimization problems and uses Ising models.

The quantum annealer devices are mainly related to implementations for optimization-related use cases and the Ising model as quantum algorithm. This is not surprising, since quantum annealers are particularly well-suited for optimization problems.
[77] describe the implementation of the problem on a quantum annealer and its hybrid solver. They try to ﬁnd the optimal portfolio of two main stock indices, the Nikkei225 and the S&P500 indices.

Venturelli and Kondratyev [78] create a hybrid algorithm (classical and quantum) and use real ﬁnancial data statistics as Phillipson and Bhatia [77] and formulate the case also as a QUBO problem. The optimized reverse annealing protocol turns out to be more than 100 times faster than the corresponding forward quantum annealing (as described by Phillipson and Bhatia [77]) on average.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: quantum SOCP interior-point method (QIPM for SOCPs)
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Kerenidis et al. [80] describe the case of positive portfolio optimization (no short selling) and budget constraints... Kerenidis et al. [80] reduce this problem to Second Order Cone Programs (SOCPs)... The problem can be further solved by considering the quantum SOCP interior-point method of Kerenidis et al. [81].

problem_solution_mappings.approach: QAOA and VQE for index tracking (variational quantum optimization)
problem_solution_mappings.quote: They describe the application of quantum optimization algorithms to index tracking. They numerically simulate the application of quantum optimization algorithms such as QAOA and VQE to this problem, and compare the performance of different quantum variational optimization algorithms in their pruning method.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: hybrid quantum/classical heuristics for Mixed Binary Optimization (MBO)
problem_solution_mappings.quote: The main contribution of Braine et al. [86] is the introduction of an approach to extend the existing quantum methods (VQE and QAOA) to more general Mixed Binary Optimization (MBO) problem classes. They use a hybrid quantum/classical heuristics to address MBO problems which allows one to model optimization with inequality constraints with a quantum computer. Furthermore, they apply this approach to the transaction settlement problem and demonstrate the performance of the corresponding algorithm on concrete instances using cloud-based quantum hardware.

They show how the relevant probability distributions can be prepared on a gate-based quantum computer in quantum superposition, the payoff functions can be implemented via quantum circuits, and the price of options can be extracted via quantum measurements. Their most important contribution is the use of the amplitude estimation (AE) algorithm, which can theoretically achieve a quadratic speed-up in the number of steps required to estimate the corresponding price compared to the Monte Carlo approach.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: gate-based AE implementations with error mitigation for option pricing
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Stamatopoulos et al. [88] extend the approach of Rebentrost et al. [40], i.e. of using AE algorithms to price options, and place a strong emphasis on implementing the algorithms in a gate-based quantum computer.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: quantum AE for economic capital requirement
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Egger et al. [96] build on this work and use a very similar approach, and thus also show a theoretical quadratic speed-up to estimate the difference between the VaR and the expected loss value. This risk measure is also known as the economic capital requirement.

problem_solution_mappings.approach: QUBO formulation and quantum annealing for crash prediction
problem_solution_mappings.quote: Orús et al. [17] propose a nonlinear network model for ﬁnancial markets to predict such ﬁnancial crashes. Their main contribution is the efﬁcient construction of a QUBO formula... They also show how to ﬁnd a solution using a quantum annealer.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing has the potential to change the financial industry by solving specific problems that are not feasible on classical hardware.
key_claims.quote: Quantum computers can solve speciﬁc problems that are not feasible on "classical" hardware. Harvesting the speed-up provided by quantum computers therefore has the potential to change any industry which uses computation, including ﬁnance.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing in finance is still in its infancy but has a wide variety of proposed applications.
key_claims.quote: Hence, there is a wide variety of proposed applications for quantum computing in the ﬁnancial industry, even though the technology is still in its infancy.
key_claims.location: Section II-E Fields of quantum computing in ﬁnance

key_claims.claim: Simulating quantum computers on classical hardware is exponentially expensive in the number of qubits and only feasible for small systems.
key_claims.quote: It follows that simulating the behavior of a quantum computer on a classical computer is exponentially expensive in terms of the number of qubits [13] and only feasible for small systems.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum hardware faces major challenges including limited qubit counts, noise, connectivity constraints, and decoherence.
key_claims.quote: However, many of the physical systems on which current quantum computers are based cannot be scaled easily. For quantum computing to ﬁnd a broader usage, more qubits are needed and the errors of actual hardware need to be reduced [10]. Besides, the physical quantum computer archi- tectures generally have constraints on qubit connectivity such as only nearest-neighbor couplings.

key_claims.claim: It is uncertain whether current leading quantum technologies will be used to create future large-scale quantum computers.
key_claims.quote: All these points render it uncertain whether the current leading quantum technologies used to create early demonstration systems will be used to create future large-scale quantum computers.

key_claims.claim: Quantum error correction will require many more qubits but is necessary for large, reliable computations.
key_claims.quote: In a similar way, the challenge that quantum gates are noisy and quickly lead to calculations which are unreliable can be tackled using quantum error correction [15]. This comes at the expense of needing even more qubits.

key_claims.claim: Open source quantum software lowers the barrier to entry and accelerates the use of quantum computing.
key_claims.quote: Another factor that needs to be mentioned when discussing quantum computer development is the availability of open source software projects that lower the barrier to learn quantum computing and thus accelerate its use.

key_claims.claim: The next ten years are expected to be the decade of quantum systems with an emerging hardware ecosystem.
key_claims.quote: The next ten years are expected to be the decade of quantum systems and the emergence of a real hardware ecosystem that will provide the foundation for improving quantum computing [19].

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing could significantly impact financial services through enhanced investment gains, reduced capital requirements, new opportunities, and improved risk management.
key_claims.quote: It was suggested in [21] that applying quantum computing in ﬁnance results in enhancing investment gains, reducing capital requirements, creating new investment op- portunities, and improving risk management and compliance.
key_claims.location: Section II-F Impact of quantum computing on the ﬁnancial industry

key_claims.claim: Quantum computing could increase cybersecurity, accelerate high-frequency trading, and improve customer relationship management.
key_claims.quote: It was stated in [23] that application of quantum computing could lead to an increase in cyber-security, accelerate high- frequency trading, or lead to greater accuracy in the simulation of customers’ purchasing preferences, resulting in an improved data-driven customer relation management.
key_claims.location: Section II-F Impact of quantum computing on the ﬁnancial industry

key_claims.claim: Breaking cryptography with quantum computers would have a major impact on the economy and could halt electronic payments and banking transactions.
key_claims.quote: Using a quantum computer to break cryptography would have a major impact on our economy and society. It is easy to follow his conclusion that a world without reliable electronic payments and banking transactions would grind to a halt.
key_claims.location: Section II-F Impact of quantum computing on the ﬁnancial industry

key_claims.claim: Widely adopted commercial quantum applications in finance may remain several years away.
key_claims.quote: This is in line with the authors of [19] who state that widely-adopted commercial applications may remain several years away.
key_claims.location: Section II-F Impact of quantum computing on the ﬁnancial industry

key_claims.claim: There are no estimates yet of how expensive it will be to maintain and run quantum computing infrastructure.
key_claims.quote: Also, there are no estimates as to how expensive maintaining the infrastructure and thus running a quantum computer will be.
key_claims.location: Section II-F Impact of quantum computing on the ﬁnancial industry

key_claims.claim: For most problems it remains open whether quantum computers have an advantage over classical computers.
key_claims.quote: Therefore, for most problems it remains open whether quan- tum computers have an advantage over classical computers.

key_claims.claim: Quantum algorithms for machine learning require full-scale quantum computers and additional hardware such as QRAM, which may be difficult to construct.
key_claims.quote: In contrast, quantum algorithms for machine learning require full-scale quantum computers and also impose additional requirements (such as the availability of quantum random access memory (QRAM), which is a quantum analogue of classical random access memory (RAM) and could be difﬁcult to construct) [25].

key_claims.claim: Gate-based quantum computers are used for both optimization and Monte Carlo use cases and mostly rely on QPE or QAE algorithms.
key_claims.quote: Gate- based quantum computers, on the other hand, cover both the optimization and Monte Carlo use cases and are mostly based on QPE or QAE algorithms.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum annealers can already approach the performance of commercial solvers on small portfolio optimization problems.
key_claims.quote: The results show that for problems of the size of the example used, certain quantum annealers in its current, still limited scope, are already able to approach the performance of the commercial solvers.

key_claims.claim: Reverse quantum annealing can be more than 100 times faster than forward quantum annealing for portfolio optimization, but speedup over classical methods is unclear.
key_claims.quote: The optimized reverse annealing protocol turns out to be more than 100 times faster than the corresponding forward quantum annealing (as described by Phillipson and Bhatia [77]) on average. However, it is not clear what increase in speed could theoretically be achieved compared to a classical approach.

key_claims.claim: Adapting QUBO formulations to allow arbitrary asset weights is an open practical issue in quantum portfolio optimization.
key_claims.quote: Another question that needs to be clariﬁed is whether the implementation of QUBO can be adapted so that assets in a portfolio can also be weighted arbitrarily, which is of more practical importance.

key_claims.claim: Quantum SOCP interior-point methods for constrained portfolio optimization have better theoretical scaling than classical methods, but speedup depends on problem parameters.
key_claims.quote: Theoretical analysis shows that the running time of this algorithm scales better than classical complexity. However, this speed-up depends on problem-dependent parameters.

key_claims.claim: Quantum alternating operator ansatz outperforms QAOA in portfolio rebalancing experiments on simulators, but quantum advantage over classical methods is not yet demonstrated.
key_claims.quote: The results of the experiments from running the algorithms on an ideal simulator highlight in particular the importance of scaling the input data for the QUAO approach and the performance advantages of the quantum alternating operator approach over it. However, further investigation is needed at several critical points to show the path from the QUAO and/or quantum alternating operator ansatz in this use case to a potential quantum advantage.

key_claims.claim: The potential theoretical speedup of QAOA-based portfolio rebalancing approaches over classical methods is not yet clear.
key_claims.quote: In particular, the potential, i. e. theoretical speed-up of these approaches compared to a classical approach is not yet clear.

key_claims.claim: AE-based quantum pricing approaches are, in principle, applicable to any derivative with payoff decomposable into elementary arithmetic operations.
key_claims.quote: Another promising point about this approach is that it can, in principle, be applied to any derivative whose payoff is a function that can be efﬁciently decomposed into elementary arithmetic operations within a quantum circuit.

key_claims.claim: Current quantum hardware is too small and noisy to evaluate typical derivative portfolios; larger devices and error correction are needed.
key_claims.quote: They came to the conclusion that much larger quantum hardware capable of running deeper quantum circuits with more qubits than currently available quantum computers is needed to evaluate typical portfolios in the ﬁnancial industry. Moreover, the results suggest that developments in quantum hardware, such as error corrections, are needed to perform practical-relevant experiments and achieve speed-up compared to current applied methods.

key_claims.claim: Experiments implementing qPCA for HJM pricing exhausted current quantum processors’ capabilities, but represent a first step toward full quantum HJM simulation.
key_claims.quote: However, the experiments exhausted the computational power offered by the current quantum processors in terms of gate ﬁdelity, connectivity and number of qubits. Nevertheless, their work is a ﬁrst step towards the development of a general quantum algorithm to fully simulate the HJM model for pricing interest rate derivatives on quantum computers.

key_claims.claim: Massive parallelization of classical Monte Carlo raises the bar for achieving quantum advantage in risk analysis.
key_claims.quote: In addition, they make another important point, namely that Monte Carlo simulations can be massively parallelised in practice, which pushes the bound for quantum advantage even higher.

key_claims.claim: Requirements for practically relevant credit risk use cases are well beyond current gate-based quantum hardware capabilities.
key_claims.quote: The requirements for such use cases are shown to be well beyond the capabilities of current gate-based quantum hardware.

key_claims.claim: Quantum computation has been demonstrated as a tool to study quantitative finance and anticipate risks, but larger processors or problem-specific annealers are needed for industry-relevant crash prediction.
key_claims.quote: According to the authors, this work can be considered the ﬁrst proof that quantum computation can be used to study quantitative ﬁnance and help institutions anticipate risks. However, a next-generation quantum processor is needed to implement larger networks and therefore relevant computations for the ﬁnancial industry. This result could be sooner achieved by developing a problem-speciﬁc quantum annealer.

key_claims.claim: It remains to be proven whether the proposed network model can predict financial crashes with high confidence.
key_claims.quote: Therefore, besides the improvement of quantum hardware, it has to be proven whether the chosen approach of the network model can indeed predict ﬁnancial crashes with high conﬁdence.

key_claims.claim: Optimization and Monte Carlo simulation are the main areas where quantum computing use cases in finance are emerging, especially portfolio construction, derivative pricing, and risk measures.
key_claims.quote: The corresponding use cases focus on the areas of optimization and Monte Carlo simulation. The ﬁrst area in particular has signiﬁcant potential in the context of investment portfolio construction. The use of quantum computing could be beneﬁcial here in that optimal portfolios can be found more quickly. In the area of Monte Carlo methods, applications are described primarily with regard to the pricing of derivatives and the estimation of risk measures such as VaR or credit default risk.

key_claims.claim: No surveyed paper describes a concrete use case for quantum-based machine learning in finance, despite ML’s importance in traditional finance.
key_claims.quote: However, no paper has been found that describes a use case for quantum-based machine learning in ﬁnance. This is somewhat surprising as machine learning already has many applications in traditional ﬁnance.

key_claims.claim: Breakthroughs in quantum hardware (more qubits, fewer errors) are necessary to realize the full potential of quantum algorithms in finance.
key_claims.quote: Nevertheless, it needs to be mentioned that breakthroughs in the development of quantum computing hardware are necessary to realize the full potential of quantum-based algorithms for ﬁnance. For example, more qubits are needed and the errors of current hardware need to be reduced.

maturity_indicators.quote: Since quantum computers are still at an early stage, quantum simulators have been developed. These are essentially software programs that run on classical computers and allow quantum programs to be executed and tested in an environment that predicts how qubits respond to operations.

Although more qubits are needed to solve more complex problems and quantum coherence (the time during which a quantum state is preserved) and topology are limited (e.g. logical operations cannot be applied to every qubit), noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers are already available to the public.

Furthermore, there is a range of open source software and quantum computer platforms publicly accessible to connect a personal computer to a quantum computer over the cloud; see, e.g., [18] for a review.
Recent demonstrations of the power of quantum computational advantage over classical computers have been constructed using superconducting qubits [8] and photonic qubits [9].
There are a variety of software libraries that can be used to simulate the behavior of qubits for different purposes.
In total, 13 papers that meet all requirements are identiﬁed and are analyzed in the next subsection.

The results of the experiments from running the algorithms on an ideal simulator highlight in particular the importance of scaling the input data for the QUAO approach and the performance advantages of the quantum alternating operator approach over it.
Furthermore, they apply this approach to the transaction settlement problem and demonstrate the performance of the corresponding algorithm on concrete instances using cloud-based quantum hardware.
Furthermore, they investigate the performance of their approach using a quantum device.
Moreover, they implement this algorithm in a quantum computer.
Woerner and Egger [10] has implemented also a small example of two assets on a real quantum-computer device.
However, these experiments also show that extensive hardware developments are still necessary for a practical application of quantum computer for derivative pricing.

open_questions.question: For which problems are current and near-term quantum computers practically useful, given real hardware constraints?
open_questions.quote: From a more practical point of view, a second question arises: for which problems are current and near-term quantum computers useful?

open_questions.question: Which problems can or cannot be solved efficiently on a quantum computer, and when do quantum computers have an advantage over classical computers?
open_questions.quote: Which problems can or cannot be solved efﬁciently on a quantum computer is still an open question in theoretical computer science, just as it is for classical computers.

open_questions.question: What is the exact quantum advantage for constraint satisfaction and combinatorial optimization problems where classical approximation techniques are improving?
open_questions.quote: Note that in the meantime there have been improvements in classical approximation techniques for the constraint satisfac- tion problems where QAOA are typically used [60]. The exact quantum advantage for these problems therefore remains an open research question.

open_questions.question: How can quantum linear systems solvers and quantum linear algebra be redesigned with reduced hardware requirements to make quantum optimization more practical?
open_questions.quote: One of the main challenges for bringing quantum optimization closer to reality is ﬁnding ways to redesign quan- tum linear systems solvers, and quantum linear algebra more generally, with reduced hardware requirements.

open_questions.question: When will quantum technology be available at scale to exploit the potential of quantum algorithms in financial services?
open_questions.quote: However, it is still very difﬁcult to estimate when the technology will be available to exploit the potential of these algorithms.
